Title: EvoSkill Injection: Red-Teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in Self-Evolving Agents
Abstract: LLM-based agent systems increasingly adopt skill-based architectures to reduce repetitive reasoning costs and improve stable, efficient task execution. Recent studies propose self-evolving agents that autonomously generate, refine, and reuse skills from past experiences to enable continuous capability evolution. However, autonomous skill evolution introduces a new attack surface in which malicious capabilities are generated, stored, and reused as legitimate skills. In this paper, we define EvoSkill Injection as a threat model targeting the autonomous skill generation and evolution pipeline of self-evolving agents. We further propose SARGE (Red-teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in self-evolving agents), a red-teaming framework for evaluating this threat model through iterative generation, escalation, and reinforcement interactions. To support our framework, we construct EvoSkillBench, a benchmark dataset of malicious interaction trajectories for inducing malicious skill formation in self-evolving agents, and introduce EvoSkillSafetyBench, a postattack benchmark for evaluating whether injected malicious skills are subsequently retrieved and activated as harmful behaviors. Our evaluation shows that SARGE induces malicious skill formation and that injected skills are persistently stored and repeatedly activated, highlighting the risk of persistent capability corruption.
Major_Contribution_Result: The paper defines EvoSkill Injection as a threat against autonomous skill generation and evolution in self-evolving agents, and presents SARGE, a red-teaming framework that iterates generation, escalation, and reinforcement interactions. It also introduces EvoSkillBench (malicious trajectories to induce malicious skill formation) and EvoSkillSafetyBench (post-attack checks of retrieval and activation of injected skills). On AutoSkill, SARGE reports attack success rates of 43.5% (Skill Generation), 54.6% (Skill Escalation), and 49.9% (Skill Reinforcement) at pass@4. The authors report that malicious skills are persistently stored and repeatedly activated across evaluated self-evolving agents and heterogeneous LLMs.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: The authors state that evaluation covers a selected set of frameworks (AutoSkill, Voyager, and ExpeL) and does not exhaustively represent all self-evolving architectures. Their multi-agent red-teaming pipeline incurs substantial compute/token cost, so GPT-4o-mini was used as the primary attack/evaluation model and stronger models may change outcomes. EvoSkillBench covers eight high-risk categories but is not complete coverage of all malicious capabilities or real-world scenarios.
Critics: This is primarily a red-teaming/benchmark contribution for self-evolving skill pipelines rather than a full defense or post-mitigation reassessment lifecycle. Reported ASR figures are tied to specific agents, attack flows, and pass@k settings, so generalization beyond those setups should stay constrained to what the paper measures. For LLM-agent security evaluation, it usefully targets persistent skill-bank corruption, but it does not by itself establish release-gate completeness across tool-use, multi-agent, or production governance settings.
